The code above contains the following key points:
• When loading the model, it is very important to set the state to eval, which has three
purposes
Turning off Dropout and BatchNorm layers. During training, Dropout layers randomly
deactivate some neurons to prevent overfitting, while BatchNorm layers dynamically
adjust normalization parameters based on the current batch of data. Once in evaluation
mode, the behavior of these layers changes: Dropout layers are deactivated and all neurons
are enabled; BatchNorm layers use the mean and variance accumulated during training
instead of the current batch’s data.
Ensure consistency. During training, certain layers (such as Dropout and BatchNorm)
behave randomly. If these layers are not turned off during evaluation, their randomness
will affect the stability and consistency of evaluation results. Using model.eval() ensures
the model behaves deterministically during evaluation, thereby providing a stable
performance evaluation.
Prevent gradient computation. Although model.eval() itself does not turn off gradient
computation, it is usually used together with torch.no_grad() to significantly reduce
memory usage and computation during evaluation. This is especially important for LLMs
(such as BERT), as they require larger memory and computation resources during inference.
• torch.no_grad() has the following three functions:
• Reduce memory usage: During evaluation, there is no need to compute gradients,
so memory usage can be reduced by torch.no_grad().
• Improve computation speed: By not computing gradients, computation speed
is increased because no backpropagation is required.
• Prevent gradient computation: During evaluation, gradients are not needed, so

The code above shows how LoRA fine-tuning is configured and executed; the next step is to explain
the main training parameters that control how the fine-tuning process behaves.
Explanation of the model fine-tuning process
The LoRA configuration parameters were introduced earlier. This subsection focuses on the training
parameters that control how the fine-tuning process runs, how often the model is evaluated, how
the learning rate is managed, and how the best checkpoint is selected.
The main training parameters are as follows:
• num_train_epochs: Defines the total number of training epochs, which controls the
duration of training. Too many epochs may lead to overfitting, while too few may lead
to underfitting. We usually use this together with an early stopping parameter to avoid
overfitting.
• per_device_train_batch_size: Sets the batch size per device (such as GPU) during
training. The batch size affects training speed and model performance.
A larger batch size can improve computational efficiency but may require more memory.
A larger batch size leads to smoother gradient updates, thus enabling more stable
convergence. However, a larger batch size may reduce the model’s generalization ability,
as it makes it easier for the model to find patterns in the training set during training, but
harder to adapt to the data distribution in the test set. Furthermore, an excessively large
batch size may cause the model to skip some local optima, thereby affecting the final
generalization ability.
A smaller batch size results in gradients with more noise since each update contains fewer
samples. This noise can sometimes help the model escape local optima, but may also
cause the training process to be unstable.
Because of their noisy characteristics, smaller batch sizes can help the model learn more
subtle differences during training, thereby improving generalization ability.
• per_device_eval_batch_size: Sets the batch size per device (such as GPU) during
evaluation (if using multiple GPUs)
• evaluation_strategy: Sets the evaluation strategy, such as steps or epoch
• steps: Evaluate the model after each step. You can obtain feedback on the model’s
performance within shorter training intervals and promptly understand its
behavior on the validation set. Since evaluations are frequent, computational
resource consumption is high. You can use this together with the early stopping
Applying Efficient Fine-Tuning Techniques to LLMs 126
mechanism to detect no improvement on the validation set sooner, and thus
stop training early to save time and resources. Frequent evaluation increases
training time, as each evaluation interrupts training to perform a full validation
set assessment.
• epoch: Evaluate the model after each epoch. Evaluation occurs less frequently,

reducing the interruption and overhead to the training process. The evaluation
results after each epoch better reflect overall changes in model performance,
reducing the impact of short-term fluctuations. However, low evaluation frequency
may lead to untimely feedback on the model’s performance during training. If a
single epoch is long, you might waste time training when performance has already
started to degrade. Although it can also be used with early stopping, if model
performance starts to deteriorate before the current epoch ends, you won’t detect
it until after the epoch, potentially wasting computational resources.
• learning_rate: The default value 3e-5 is commonly used as the initial learning rate for
fine-tuning many pre-trained transformer models (such as BERT) on downstream tasks.
For BERT-base fine-tuning, 3e-5 is a common starting learning rate. Smaller datasets
often need a smaller value, such as 1e-5, to reduce the risk of overfitting, while larger
datasets can sometimes use a higher value, such as 5e-5. The grid search and random
search techniques discussed below can be used to tune from this starting point.
In general, a larger learning rate can speed up convergence, but it may also cause unstable
training or make the model oscillate near local optima. A smaller learning rate is usually
more stable, but it may require more training time.
• lr_scheduler_type: For most fine-tuning tasks, especially when you want the learning
rate to smoothly decrease, you can use linear. If you need to adjust the learning rate
periodically during training, such as for longer training tasks, you can use cosine. To
find the most suitable learning rate, you can perform a learning rate search using the
following methods:
• Grid Search: Perform a grid search within a predefined range of learning rates to
find the optimal value.
• Random Search: Perform a random search within a predefined range of learning

• Learning Rate Decay: Gradually reduce the learning rate during training to find

The contract classification example shows how LoRA can fine-tune a model efficiently by updating
only a small set of parameters. However, as model size increases, memory usage and computational
cost can still become major constraints. The next section introduces the quantization techniques
used in QLoRA, which further reduce storage and memory requirements by lowering numerical
precision while preserving as much model performance as possible.
Applying quantization techniques in QLoRA
Quantization is a technique for reducing computational and storage requirements by representing
model parameters with lower numerical precision. In deep learning, model parameters are often
represented as 32-bit floating-point values, which require significant memory and compute
resources. By converting these values to lower-precision formats, such as 16-bit floating-point
values or 8-bit integers, quantization can reduce memory usage and improve efficiency. However,
effective quantization is more complex than simply truncating decimal places, because overly
aggressive precision reduction can reduce model accuracy. In QLoRA, quantization relies on several
related steps and techniques, including normalization, integer quantization, dequantization, and
blockwise quantization, to reduce memory usage while preserving sas much model performance
as possible.
The first step is to scale the original floating-point values into a range that can be represented
more efficiently in a lower-precision format.
Normalization
Normalization is applied to input data to scale its values into a target range. For example, 32-bit
floating-point (FP32) tensors can be normalized to the range [-127, 127]. Compared to simple
decimal truncation, normalization better preserves model accuracy.

Normalization, quantization, and dequantization describe the basic conversion process. However,
model weights are not always distributed evenly, so applying one scale across a large tensor can
produce errors when outliers are present. Blockwise quantization addresses this by quantizing
smaller blocks independently.
Blockwise quantization
To address possible outlier issues during quantization, the input data can be divided into blocks,
with each block being quantized independently. This method improves quantization accuracy
when the data distribution is uneven.
In practical applications, particularly in neural network model compression and acceleration,
quantization is often used in combination with multiple techniques to minimize loss of model
accuracy. There are mainly three approaches.
Mixed Precision Quantization: Using different quantization precisions in different layers or
modules.
Post-Training Quantization: Performing quantization after the model training is completed to
reduce computation and storage requirements.
Quantization Aware Training: Considering quantization effects during the training process and
directly optimizing the performance of the quantized model.

Applications with RAG and
Multi-Agent Systems
Modern LLMs (GPT-5, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and others) have profoundly
transformed the field of natural language processing, bringing about numerous breakthroughs.
However, these models often face a range of challenges when addressing specific enterprise needs,
especially in terms of data security, accuracy, and domain expertise.
Against this backdrop, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) technology has emerged. By
combining traditional information retrieval with advanced text generation, this technology
effectively enhances model performance and applicability in specific business scenarios. This
chapter aims to systematically introduce the working principles of RAG technology and its
application cases in enterprises, helping readers gain an in-depth understanding of how to deploy
this technology in daily business operations.
In this chapter, we will be covering the following topics:
• Understanding the core workflow of RAG
• Addressing enterprise constraints with RAG
• Applying RAG to enterprise question-answering scenarios
• Generating SQL with RAG2SQL
• Coordinating complex tasks with multi-agent systems
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 138
Understanding the core workflow of RAG
RAG is one of the most important patterns for building enterprise-ready LLM applications because
it allows a model to generate answers using external, organization-specific knowledge rather
than relying only on what it learned during training. To understand how RAG works, it is useful
to begin with its two core components—the retriever and the generator—and then examine how
data moves through the indexing, retrieval, and generation stages of the workflow.
Core components of RAG
RAG is a natural language processing technology that combines information retrieval and text
generation. By integrating information from large-scale datasets, RAG enhances the output of
generative models, enabling them to provide more comprehensive, accurate, and detailed answers.
This technology has broad application potential in areas such as question answering systems,
chatbots, and content generation.
Its core components include the Retriever and the Generator:
• The Retriever is responsible for quickly retrieving the most relevant information from vast
document collections or datasets based on the user’s query. It uses efficient indexing and
query techniques, such as inverted indexes or the latest vector search methods, to ensure
that the most relevant results are returned in the shortest possible time.

• The Generator is responsible for generating coherent, relevant, and information-rich text
based on the retrieved information. Advanced language models such as GPT or BERT are
commonly used, combined with the content from retrieved documents, to generate text
directly related to the user’s query.
Together, the retriever and generator form the foundation of a RAG system. The retriever identifies
the information most relevant to the user’s query, while the generator uses that information to
produce a grounded response. The next step is to look at how these components work together
across the full RAG workflow.

Chapter 5 139
RAG workflow
The RAG workflow is shown in Figure 5.1 and is divided into the data indexing stage, retrieval
stage, and generation stage.
Figure 5.1: RAG workflow
1. Data indexing stage
The data indexing stage mainly uses embedding models to convert different types of data into
vectors and store them in a vector database. Common vector database choices include Milvus
and Weaviate (self-hosted, open source), Pinecone (managed cloud), and pgvector (PostgreSQL
extension for teams already using Postgres). LlamaIndex and LangChain support all of these
via consistent interfaces. For text data, use a dedicated embedding model trained for retrieval
— sentence-transformers (open source), OpenAI text-embedding-3 (commercial), or BGE-M3
(open source, multilingual). Plain BERT is a feature extractor and underperforms purpose-built
embedding models on retrieval tasks.
2. Retrieval stage
In the retrieval stage, the user’s input query is converted into a vector, which is then matched for
similarity with the data in the vector database to find the most relevant data.
1. Document segmentation: First, long textual documents in large-scale datasets are
segmented into smaller, more manageable, and easily searchable chunks
2. Semantic similarity check: Natural language processing tools are used to analyze
the semantic similarity between the user’s query and each document chunk, quickly
pinpointing the most relevant information
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 140
Once the most relevant document chunks have been retrieved, the system can pass them to the
generator to produce a response grounded in the retrieved context.
3. Generation stage
In the generation stage, the retrieved data is passed to the generator, which produces the final
output based on the retrieved data and the user’s query.
1. Text Matching and Relevance: Based on retrieval results, the generator evaluates the
relevance of the information and constructs answers according to the user’s specific needs
2. Diversity and Uniqueness: When generating answers, focus is placed on the diversity
and uniqueness of content to avoid generating generic or repetitive text, ensuring output
quality and personalization
In addition, even for text data, there are various file formats, such as Text, Word, PDF, etc., which
require different processing methods. Currently, LlamaIndex provides a variety of tools to
conveniently handle these different file formats.
After understanding the basic RAG workflow, the next question is why enterprises need this
approach in the first place. RAG is especially useful in business environments where models must
work with private data, produce evidence-based answers, and apply domain-specific knowledge
that may not be available in the model’s original training data.

Addressing enterprise constraints with RAG
Enterprise application scenarios usually include three types of constraints: data security
requirements, data accuracy requirements, and domain knowledge requirements:
• Data security requirements: Enterprises usually possess large amounts of data with strict
data security requirements that must not be disclosed to external parties
• Data accuracy requirements: The output of LLMs must be evidence-based
• Domain knowledge requirements: The meaning represented by enterprise data is often
unique to vertical domains, making it difficult for general LLMs to provide answers based
on domain knowledge

The advantages of RAG technology are shown in Figure 5.2.
Figure 5.2: Advantages of RAG technology
As shown in Figure 5.2, RAG is useful because it connects three elements that are often difficult to
align in enterprise AI applications: the user’s intent, the knowledge already contained in the LLM,
and external enterprise data. Without retrieval, an LLM may generate plausible but unsupported
answers, increasing the risk of hallucination. Without an intent-aware search layer, enterprise data
may remain difficult to retrieve accurately, even when the relevant information exists. Without
RAG, organizations may also rely too heavily on fine-tuning, which can introduce additional
cost, hardware requirements, and maintenance overhead. By retrieving relevant external data at
query time and providing it to the model as context, RAG helps generate answers that are more
grounded, accurate, and aligned with enterprise-specific knowledge.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 142
Under the three types of constraints mentioned above, RAG technology can effectively address
enterprise pain points and meet their needs.
After explaining why RAG is well suited to enterprise constraints, the next step is to see how it
works in practical business scenarios. Question-answering systems are a natural starting point
because they require the model to understand user intent, retrieve relevant enterprise knowledge,
and generate responses that are accurate, contextual, and useful to the user.
Applying RAG to enterprise question-answering
scenarios
RAG is especially useful in enterprise question-answering scenarios because it allows an LLM
to retrieve relevant business knowledge before generating a response. This section looks at two
examples: a customer service Q&A system that uses historical voice and answer data, and a
wealth management assistant that helps client managers retrieve and apply financial, product,
and customer information.
Building a customer service Q&A system
A certain bank has accumulated a large amount of customer service Q&A voice data over the past
several years, containing customers’ questions and customer service responses. The bank hopes
to leverage this data to build an intelligent customer service Q&A system to help customers solve
problems more quickly and accurately.
(1) Speech recognition
Converting customer voice input into text data is the first step of the process, as the original voice
data needs to be transformed into text for subsequent processing and understanding. By using
existing high-accuracy speech recognition technologies, such as the API service interface from the
OpenAI Whisper API, Google Cloud Speech-to-Text, or Microsoft Azure Speech, or offline models
such as Whisper or Distil-Whisper for self-hosted deployments, customers’ spoken questions

can be transcribed into text.
(2) Text preprocessing
Cleaning and standardizing the text data after speech recognition includes removing stop
words, correcting spelling errors, and standardizing grammar. First, leverage the contextual
understanding capabilities of LLMs to fix obvious errors; second, further improve the quality and
accuracy of the text through manual proofreading.

Chapter 5 143
(3) Applying RAG technology
Apply RAG technology, which combines retrieval and generation, to first retrieve the most relevant
content from a large-scale knowledge base, and then generate answers based on this content. This
process is realized through two stages. The first stage is to construct a question bank and a standard
answer bank, quickly finding standard answers most related to the question through retrieval
techniques. In this process, LLMs are used to generate multiple similar questions, improving
retrieval coverage. The second stage is to use the comprehension ability of LLMs to retrieve the
customer’s own information (such as purchased product information, latest interaction records,
etc.) based on the question.
(4) Generating answers
The purpose of answer generation is to produce accurate and human-friendly responses, and
to achieve personalized feedback based on the retrieval results, allowing the model to continue
training to adapt to specific business and language usage, thereby improving the relevance and
accuracy of the responses.
(5) Post-processing and feedback loop
Through post-processing and a feedback loop, response quality, and system performance can
be optimized. This involves grammar correction and style adjustment for generated answers to
ensure professionalism and accuracy. At the same time, feedback on customer satisfaction with
the answers is sent back into the system for continual learning and improvement of the model.
The same RAG pattern can also be applied beyond customer service. In knowledge-intensive
domains such as wealth management, RAG can help professionals retrieve client information,
product details, market knowledge, and past interaction records to support more personalized
responses.
Supporting wealth management with RAG
In the field of wealth management, RAG has a wide range of applications, from client managers’
customer management to clients’ wealth management, and all can utilize RAG technology.
The following takes the pain points of a client manager as an example to describe the specific
application of RAG in this field. The background is: Alice Summers is a wealth client manager at
a financial institution, responsible for managing the contact information of over 1,000 clients.
Her customer management tasks mainly include the following:
• Regularly contacting clients to understand their latest needs and investment intentions
• Providing personalized investment advice based on clients’ needs and risk preferences
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 144
• Timely answering clients’ questions and resolving their issues
• Regularly sending clients the latest financial market news and investment advice
• Tracking clients’ investment situations to adjust portfolios in a timely manner

• High similarity of data; similar products have subtle differences, and the documents are

• Large amount of data and frequent updates, requiring efficient retrieval and updating

In the data processing workflow, only after solving these issues can we ensure the accuracy and
efficiency of subsequent retrieval and generation processes. To address the above problems, we
can take advantage of some open-source tools. For example, the LlamaIndex framework provides

An example of the LlamaIndex toolkit is shown in Figure 5.5.

• Focusing on vertical application scenarios performs better than generalized scenarios.
Through wealth product evaluation, when data and metrics are clearly defined, the

• Clarify the requirements for models and hardware resources. A model with 7.2 billion

Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 148
After looking at how RAG can support enterprise question-answering scenarios, the chapter now
turns to a more structured data problem: generating SQL from natural language questions. In
many organizations, valuable business information is stored in databases, but users often need
knowledge of table structures, field meanings, and query logic to access it. RAG2SQL applies the
retrieval-and-generation pattern to this problem by combining database metadata, historical SQL
examples, and natural language understanding to help generate SQL that matches enterprise-
specific data logic.
Generating SQL with RAG2SQL
Text-to-SQL refers to the process of converting a user’s natural language question into a SQL
query that can be executed against a structured database. For example, a user might ask, “Which
products had the highest sales last quarter?” and the system must translate that request into a
valid SQL statement that selects the right tables, fields, filters, and aggregation logic. This task
is more difficult than ordinary text retrieval because the model must understand both the user’s
intent and the database schema, then produce SQL that is syntactically correct and consistent
with the organization’s business rules.
Generating SQL from natural language is one of the more structured applications of RAG because
the model must understand both the user’s question and the organization’s database logic. Unlike
general text generation, RAG2SQL depends on schema information, metadata, business definitions,

historical SQL examples, and result validation. This section explains why enterprise text-to-SQL
is difficult, then uses Vanna AI as an example framework to show how RAG can support SQL
generation, workflow design, domain-specific retrieval, and iterative improvement.
Understanding the enterprise Text-to-SQL problem
With the rise of LLM technology, programmers have been among the first to experience the
revolutionary changes in code development, ranging from autocompletion to the automatic
generation of module functionalities. However, in the database domain, despite its vast potential,
there have not yet been breakthrough advances. The main challenges lie in the diversity and
complexity of enterprise databases: each company’s database structure, table design, and
statistical processing logic are unique, and this information is seldom shared on open-source
platforms such as GitHub.
To address these challenges, organizations can combine locally deployed LLMs, database metadata,
business definitions, and historical SQL examples in a RAG workflow. This allows the system to
retrieve relevant schema information and prior query patterns before generating SQL that aligns
with enterprise-specific business logic. The widespread application of this technology will bring
great convenience to data analysts and big data platform operations and management personnel.

Using Vanna AI as a RAG2SQL example
Currently, the open-source software provider Vanna � ai has released its foundational RAG2SQL
framework on GitHub. This framework achieves high-precision SQL generation on complex
datasets through several key features:
• RAG framework: By integrating retrieval-augmented generation technology, it enhances
the accuracy of generated SQL statements
• LLMs: Utilize advanced LLMs to understand complex query requirements
• High-quality training data: Trained on abundant data to improve the quality of generated
SQL statements
• Continuous optimization capabilities: The framework supports continual learning and
optimization to adapt to ever-changing data environments
• Broad database support: Compatible with various types of databases and frontend
technologies
• Open-source customization: Allows users to customize and optimize the framework
based on specific requirements
The Vanna AI framework has wide-ranging application scenarios, covering business intelligence,
medical research, education, and other fields, suitable for any situation that requires efficient
data query and analysis. With improvements in natural language processing capabilities, users
can submit query requests in natural language, which the system automatically translates into
SQL statements and executes in the database to retrieve the required data.
Following the RAG2SQL workflow
These capabilities come together in a workflow that retrieves relevant schema, metadata, and
SQL examples before generating and validating a query.
Several frameworks can be used to explore this pattern. The following discussion
uses Vanna AI as one representative open-source example of how RAG can be applied
to natural language-to-SQL generation.
Building Enterprise AI Applications with RAG and Multi-Agent Systems 150
The workflow of RAG2SQL based on the Vanna AI framework is shown in Figure 5.7.
Figure 5.7: Workflow of RAG2SQL based on the Vanna AI framework
This system is used to convert natural language queries into SQL queries, which are executed
to obtain data, and then the results are validated and processed. The workflow consists of the
following main steps:
1. Raise the Question: The user raises a question, which is the starting point of the process
2. Search: The system searches for relevant information by querying databases, documents,
or other stored answers. This step may involve accessing data indexes and can use vector
searches or other advanced search technologies.
3. Prompt Generation: Based on the information found during the search, the system
generates one or more SQL query prompts. This could involve understanding and parsing
natural language queries, then converting them into structured queries.
4. Execute SQL Query: The system constructs SQL queries based on the generated prompts

that supports SQL.

5. Result Verification: The system presents the query results to the user and checks whether
the user’s needs are met. This may include data frames, charts, or AI-generated follow-
up questions.
6. Result Feedback: If the results are correct, the process ends and the user obtains the
required information; if not, the user can perform a manual query or rewrite the question,
and the system may learn and adjust according to the feedback
After the overall workflow is clear, it is useful to look more closely at the RAG-specific features
that support SQL generation and domain knowledge retrieval.
Examining RAG-specific features
Under this framework, Vanna AI has implemented two features:
• A RAG model is trained based on provided SQL historical code. The entire process requires
manual problem construction, restoring the code’s function into natural language
descriptions, as shown in Figure 5.8.

• A RAG-based domain knowledge information retrieval tool is constructed, for example,
using various business metadata and statistical metric descriptions from big data systems.
To improve retrieval accuracy, an additional classification model is trained to identify
the information category associated with each query and to further retrieve and provide
accurate information to the LLM based on the classification results. The RAG2SQL retrieval
filtering process is shown in Figure 5.9.

Although this framework shows how RAG can support SQL generation, practical deployment
still depends on framework maturity, model access, metadata quality, annotation effort, and the
surrounding AI infrastructure.
Recognizing current system limitations
The current system also has some shortcomings or areas to be optimized, mainly in the following
aspects:
• Currently, the framework is in its initial stage, and the functional modules are not yet
complete or robust.
• It relies on API-based calls to commercial LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google),
which may not be available or affordable in all deployment environments. Self-hosted
alternatives (Llama, Mistral, Qwen, or other open-weight models) require additional
integration work that the framework does not yet provide out of the box.

• Cost and latency should also be considered when choosing a deployment model. As a
rough order-of-magnitude estimate, a lightweight commercial-API RAG query that uses
an embedding model plus a small or mid-sized LLM may cost around $0.001–$0.005 per
query and return in about 1–3 seconds, depending on prompt length, retrieved context
size, model choice, and network conditions. A self-hosted equivalent using an open-
source embedding model and an open-weight LLM can reduce marginal per-query cost
after infrastructure is in place, but it requires GPU capacity, deployment engineering,
monitoring, scaling, and ongoing maintenance.
• The training process involves quite a few data governance factors, such as the completeness
of metadata.
• During training, many samples require manual annotation, such as reverse-translating
code into natural language descriptions, etc.
• Relying on relatively complete AI foundational platforms, such as vector data, embedding
model selection, customized classification model design and training, etc.
If the above issues can be resolved, the implementation of RAG2SQL technology will bring
tremendous long-term value.
Several of the RAG2SQL challenges discussed above involve coordinating multiple steps, including
retrieval, prompt generation, SQL execution, result verification, feedback, metadata management,
and integration with supporting tools. These are exactly the kinds of multi-step workflows that
multi-agent frameworks are designed to help organize. The next section introduces multi-agent
systems and shows how a framework such as CrewAI can structure a pipeline in which different
agents take on different roles, use tools, pass outputs to one another, and collaborate toward a
final result.
Coordinating complex tasks with multi-agent systems
The RAG2SQL framework workflow covers multiple tasks, from data sample preparation and
classification model training to generated result evaluation. Currently, the latest LLMs are
attempting to automate various processes through multi-agent systems. There are already
more than a dozen multi-agent systems, such as Microsoft’s AutoGen, LangChain agents (built
using the LangChain framework), CrewAI, etc. These systems share the common feature of
decomposing the output of LLMs into multiple tasks, each accomplished by different agents.
This method can improve the efficiency and accuracy of the system, while better adapting to
different business scenarios.

Using CrewAI as an example multi-agent framework
In some scenarios, this concept has already seen initial applications. Figure 5.10 shows an
application case of the CrewAI framework.
Figure 5.10: Application case of the CrewAI framework
CrewAI is a multi-agent system framework that allows developers to create teams composed

of multiple agents that can collaborate to accomplish complex tasks. The design of the CrewAI
framework is inspired by human team collaboration, where each agent can take on different roles
and focus on specific tasks or domains. Below are some key features of the CrewAI framework:
• Role-playing agents: In CrewAI, each agent is assigned a role, such as database expert,
technical writer, or quality assurance specialist, and performs tasks according to its role
and objectives
Several frameworks can be used to build multi-agent workflows, including AutoGen,
LangChain agents, CrewAI, and similar orchestration tools. The following example

tasks, tools, and processes can be combined into a collaborative workflow.

• Tool usage: Agents can utilize predefined tools or custom tools to accomplish tasks, such as
searching the internet, parsing websites, or performing document retrieval and generation
• Process control: CrewAI provides various process control options, including sequential
execution, hierarchical management, and consensus mechanisms, to coordinate task

and clear task definitions to improve system efficiency and reliability
• Environment Integration: CrewAI can be integrated with external environments such
as the OpenAI API, and can also be used with local models
• Error Handling and Robustness: CrewAI provides error handling mechanisms to help
agents recover when encountering problems

From development to implementation, software must go through several stages, including

data silos and system silos exist between each stage, inevitably leading to conflicts. Furthermore,

DevOps, SRE (Site Reliability Engineering), and Platform Engineering serve as the three
foundational cornerstones of software delivery. Like links in a chain, they orchestrate engineers’
work across different platforms, enabling multi-platform collaboration and allowing engineers to
complete software delivery more efficiently and enjoyably. In addition, they provide enterprises
with a range of objective data, allowing for real-time analysis of weak links in the delivery process,

Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 164
Improving software delivery with DevOps
DevOps is one of the main foundations of modern software delivery because it connects the people,
processes, tools, and feedback loops involved in turning software ideas into reliable business value.

Rather than treating development, testing, operations, and business teams as separate groups
working in sequence, DevOps encourages them to collaborate across the full delivery lifecycle. In
this section, we examine how DevOps supports enterprise goals, connects IT capability domains,
improves delivery visibility, shifts quality and risk management earlier in the lifecycle, strengthens
digital operations, and extends into newer practices such as MLOps and LLMOps.
The three pillars discussed in this chapter are practices and operating models rather
than single tools. In real organizations, they are usually implemented through a
combination of automation, infrastructure, observability, incident management,
and internal-platform tools. The following examples provide a practical starting

The concept of DevOps
DevOps (a combination of Development and Operations) is a collective term for the processes,
methods, and systems used to facilitate communication, collaboration, and integration between
software development, IT operations, and quality assurance departments, as shown in Figure 6.2.
Professionals in the software industry have gradually realized that, in order to deliver software
products or services on time, developers and operations staff must work closely together, focus
on communication, and speed up, reliably build, test, and release software through automated
processes.
Figure 6.2: Scope of DevOps
In recent years, DevOps has been implemented across various industries, sectors, and enterprises
of different sizes, achieving good practical results. For enterprises aiming at lean operation and IT
lean management, the original concepts of DevOps can no longer meet their needs, giving rise to
disruptive development and transformation. Improving organizational-level efficiency and quality
has become a new direction for capabilities output in the development of DevOps. Therefore,
besides its original role in facilitating inter-departmental communication, DevOps now elevates
full lifecycle management of applications to a new level. At the same time, corresponding cultural
collaboration and process-driven approaches have advanced alongside data-driven capabilities,
achieving a highly collaborative goal in technical operations and value delivery.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 166
For enterprise users, it is essential to clearly explain what DevOps is, what its core objectives are,
and what capabilities should be possessed, as this directly relates to enterprise-level practice
and implementation. The author has discussed with members and individuals from multiple
relevant organizations in the industry, and though their feedback varied, the core value remains
consistent—how to achieve ultimate value delivery and output through DevOps.
To understand this value more clearly, DevOps needs to be viewed not only as a technical practice
but also as an enterprise capability. Its impact depends on how well it supports business goals
and how effectively IT organizations use it to coordinate delivery, operations, and continuous
improvement.
The relationship among DevOps, enterprises, and IT
organizations
DevOps sits between enterprise strategy and IT execution. At the enterprise level, it helps
organizations improve delivery speed, quality, and responsiveness to market needs. At the IT
organization level, it provides a way to coordinate teams, standardize processes, automate delivery
activities, and create feedback loops across the software lifecycle. The following discussion looks
at both relationships in turn.
The relationship between DevOps and enterprises

The development of enterprises requires clear goals, which are usually measured by economic
benefits. Economic benefits include productivity, turnover, profit margin, and return on investment.
The development goals of an enterprise can be described from the following four aspects:
• The enterprise’s contribution goals to society. For different types and business models of
enterprises, the enterprise’s contribution goals to society are reflected in the effectiveness
and benefits of their products.
• The enterprise’s market goals. The market goals determine whether an enterprise can
survive. Improving the innovation level of products, the ability to bring products to market
quickly, and a product’s market share are important means to achieve the enterprise’s
market goals.
• The enterprise’s development goals. The development goals are key for enterprises to
improve productivity. They are achieved by expanding enterprise scale, increasing fixed
assets and working capital, enhancing production capacity, increasing product variety,
output, and sales, improving per capita productivity, and raising automation levels.

• The enterprise’s profit goals. In the course of business operations, an enterprise aims to
maximize its profit goals through cost reduction and efficiency enhancement. “Cost
reduction and efficiency enhancement” can be achieved by product adjustments and
internal management changes, based on internal and external data analysis and support.
The positioning of DevOps in enterprise development is more about creating added value
than achieving miracles in desperate situations. When implementing enterprise-level DevOps,
managers should note that regardless of whether the enterprise is undergoing business model
transformation, digital transformation, or brand management transformation, it must use
advanced information technology to enhance management levels and improve competitiveness—
this is precisely the value and capability that DevOps provides.
In terms of core value output, DevOps acts as a “catalyst,” which does not conflict with the
enterprise’s development goals. Therefore, regardless of whether DevOps implementation is
successful, it will not cause a fundamental change in the enterprise, but it can bring commercial
success.
The relationship between DevOps and IT organizations
The IT organization is the carrier for enterprise-level DevOps practice. For enterprises, day-to-day
operations cannot proceed without the cooperation and support of IT organizations. Typically,
IT organizations are essential components for an enterprise’s sustainable operation, possessing
informatization and digitization attributes. In daily business activities, IT organizations are
required to have the following two core capabilities:
• Guided by the company’s strategic objectives, support enterprise strategy through
informatization and digitalization means
• Under the guidance of the overall informatization planning, build informatization and
digital infrastructure and application systems to provide technical support for enterprise
operations
The “entanglement” between IT organizations and DevOps originates from the IT organization’s
self-reform. In most enterprises, the pressures faced by IT organizations can be divided into
internal and external pressures. Internal pressure mainly comes from internal management
and coordination, while external pressure mainly arises from the service demands of business
departments. When external pressure needs to be relieved through internal management, the
innate capabilities of DevOps cannot cover all requirements. Today, more and more enterprises
are turning to DevOps. In addition to utilizing DevOps to improve efficiency and maintain high
standards and high-efficiency output, it is also necessary to ensure the rationality of external
pressure release. Some large internet companies, such as Netflix, Spotify, and Etsy, have achieved
