chunks.heading: Chapter 6 167
chunks.content:
good results in this area in their practice.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 168
With scale and capability expansion, IT organizations develop from an “individual contributor
model” to a “multi-team coordination model,” leading to the division of responsibilities and the
connection of workflows—what we commonly refer to as IT organizational capability sub-domains,
such as project management, requirement management, product management, architecture
management, development management, testing management, operations management, and
security management within the delivery chain. In the delivery chain, capability sub-domains
exist as single nodes. While collaborating and connecting, there are goal conflicts beyond their
responsibilities.
Therefore, within IT organizations, DevOps must achieve seamless IT service processes and
resolve the contradictions among various capability sub-domains. This is an extension of DevOps’
innate capabilities. The focus here is on online collaboration across departments and teams,
and the delivery of information along the delivery pipeline through the DevOps philosophy. For
example, when deploying a system online using traditional methods, a lengthy explanation
document may be needed; whereas by using DevOps methods for system deployment, automated
deployment can be achieved through standard runtime environment selection, environment
setup, and orchestration of the deployment process. Additionally, such deployment methods
can be understood by operators, executed by machines, and the deployment process can also be
tracked and audited.
These examples show that DevOps is not only about improving collaboration between development
and operations. In larger IT organizations, it must also address the friction created by separate
capability domains, disconnected tools, and handoffs across the delivery pipeline. This makes
conflict resolution and delivery-chain integration the next steps in understanding DevOps at
enterprise scale.
Resolving conflicts and connecting the delivery chain
Resolving conflicts among capability sub-domains is the foundation; connecting application
lifecycle management and value delivery is the next step. For instance, from project initiation,
requirement collection, architecture design, code development, integration and build, code testing,
continuous deployment, code configuration, to go-live monitoring—the integration of toolsets,
followed by unified toolchains, and ultimately achieving the monetization of IT organizational
capabilities.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 169
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 169
IT organizations need to achieve technology output and technology operations through DevOps
capabilities, with the following two characteristics:
• When IT organizations have business attributes, DevOps can create value
• Even when IT organizations do not have business attributes, DevOps can still contribute
value
After examining DevOps from the perspectives of enterprise value, IT organizations, and delivery-
chain integration, we can now define it more precisely. DevOps is not just a set of tools or a
simple merger of development and operations; it is a methodology for improving organizational
effectiveness, delivery quality, and value flow across the software lifecycle.
Defining DevOps as a delivery methodology
So what exactly is DevOps? On the surface, DevOps refers to the integration of development
and operations, which is also the native capability of DevOps—that is, using tools to help
developers perform some of the work of operations personnel, thereby reducing costs. However,
after we gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between DevOps, enterprises, and IT
organizations, we find that DevOps is actually a methodology —an organizational effectiveness
and quality management methodology. In the delivery pipeline capability subdomain, DevOps
removes barriers; in the project and requirements subdomain, DevOps enables precise process
control and risk management; in the software development and testing subdomain, DevOps
helps development and testing teams improve delivery efficiency while ensuring quality; in the
operations subdomain, DevOps enhances the efficiency of product releases and accelerates online
quality feedback.
Meanwhile, by using delivery pipeline tools to realize data collection and by managing the process
through metrics for feedback and optimization, organizational effectiveness and quality are
ultimately improved.
Once DevOps is understood as a methodology for improving organizational effectiveness and
delivery quality, the next step is to examine the capabilities that make this improvement possible
in practice. These capabilities include visualizing delivery data, shifting quality and security
activities earlier in the lifecycle, operating through data-driven feedback, improving collaboration,
and managing delivery-related risk.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 170
Digital visualization capabilities in DevOps
During the software delivery process, digital visualization possesses two capabilities: visualization
capability oriented toward the Terminal and visualization capability oriented toward the
environment. The ultimate effect depends on the final “destination” of software delivery, which
is what we often refer to as value.
Digital visualization terminal
As the most fundamental capability of IT organizations, many believe that the “terminal” target

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 169
chunks.content:
of digital visualization is the enterprise leadership. However, this is a misunderstanding. The
targets of digital visualization not only include the management and business operations levels
of the enterprise but also a large number of backend support organizations and all components
of the enterprise. This is key to the management of people, finance, and assets in the enterprise.
In addition to personnel, processes, resources, and decisions also need to leverage digital means
for data visualization support. For enterprises, the value of “people, finance, and assets” must
always serve the business. Therefore, the ultimate value of digital visualization lies in the service
value based on positive business feedback, which is similar to the measurement and indicator
systems of DevOps. Digital visualization provides decision support for the business and serves
as a basis for management improvement.
Digital visualization ultimately needs to return to the Terminal; here, the Terminal refers to the
object that promotes lean enterprise operations through digital visualization, including business
operations and IT operations. The Terminal uses the positive feedback capability of data to achieve
problem location and assist decision-making. Digital visualization presents the value of data,
while the Terminal needs to reflect and act based on the presented content.
In the actual process of data visualization, it is necessary to clarify the beneficiary, decision object,
metrics, and goals of data visualization.
Digital visualization scenarios
The Scenario of digital visualization is aimed at comprehensive digital enterprise management,
focusing on people, finance, and assets, with the business at the center. When planning a digital
visualization Scenario, it is necessary to specify the particular problem the Scenario can solve,
and, at the same time, ensure the Scenario can match the analytical conclusions and data paths.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 171
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 171
Here is a simple example for illustration: before a product goes into operation, software is delivered
via DevOps. The speed and quality of software delivery directly affect the product’s post-launch
performance in the market. Thus, IT lean operation holds an important position in comprehensive
digital management. When IT is the core component of business, IT is direct productivity. When
IT is not a core business component, the value of IT is still to enable better enterprise operations;
therefore, IT lean operation and enterprise business value are interconnected. The best practice
DevOps metrics system covers enterprise cost management and evaluation management. Within
the resources and cost framework, it forms a deep scenario management capability for IT activities
and establishes a data-related information view, as shown in Figure 6.3.
Figure 6.3: DevOps scenario hierarchy
In the field of business operations, digital visualization needs to clearly identify the factors that
affect performance, commonly referred to as intelligent operations. Data is categorized by scenario,
usually including sales data, order data, user activity data, production capacity data, and product
data, and data performance is matched to evaluation metrics. For business operations, data
performance is a potential driving factor for business development trends; any data deviation may
affect whether the business progresses as planned. This form of visualization related to business
trends is referred to as a scenario in the digital visualization field. By analyzing data performance,
problems in business operations can be identified, and based on the driving factors, decision-
making can be assisted to make targeted adjustments and improvements.
Visualization gives teams the information they need to understand delivery performance and
business impact. The next capability is shift-left practice, where DevOps uses that information
earlier in the lifecycle to improve quality, security, and delivery outcomes before problems reach
production.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 172
DevOps technology shift-left capabilities
In the vast majority of enterprises, whether considered from the perspective of a profit center
or a cost center, the role of IT in business activities is increasingly moving forward. Especially
in scenarios where market demands change rapidly, delivering software that is “secure, stable,
efficient, and low-cost” enables enterprises to better respond to market fluctuations and deliver
business value. Therefore, technology infrastructure centered on DevOps has gradually become
the core of IT management in enterprise digital transformation and is also a focal point of practice
for traditional enterprises in the process of software delivery.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 171
chunks.content:
New technology infrastructure
The new technological infrastructure of enterprises is represented by innovative technologies
such as DevOps, cloud computing, microservices, and artificial intelligence. At the objective
level, DevOps aligns IT organizations with business organizations, focusing on business value
and customer experience; at the cultural level, it promotes a high-trust cultural philosophy,
fostering seamless communication, and shared risk between IT, business, and other functional
organizations; at the technological empowerment level, it combines technology, and capabilities
to realize intelligent, agile, and digital platforms.
Best practices of DevOps in the IT field effectively achieve a shift-left for internal enterprise IT,
bringing products to market better and faster through cost efficiency, increased productivity,
and quality assurance, assisting business organizations in building systematic capabilities, and
increasing innovation and risk resistance of products through business innovation and exceptional
user experience.
The extent to which DevOps shifts left depends on IT’s influence in business operations as well
as the scope of its capability output. The role of DevOps in the process of enterprise digital
transformation is largely determined by the reshaping of IT leadership. IT leaders must have
forward-looking thinking and grasp strategies that drive digital transformation, providing
necessary IT services and products for enterprise digital transformation. Additionally, there is a
need to integrate IT resources, organizational structure, and technological innovation according
to enterprise strategic objectives, so that IT service capabilities are maximally oriented toward
business, creating the greatest value and achieving the goal of upgrading IT management in
digital transformation.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 173
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 173
Application modernization
Application modernization is also an effective way to shift technology left. Application
modernization is a novel concept that leverages existing legacy applications to modernize the
underlying platform infrastructure, internal architecture, and functionality. Conceptually, it
is similar to low-code approaches. According to McKinsey Digital’s COVID recovery research,
enterprises with low digitalization levels suffered greater losses during the pandemic, while those
with a higher degree of digitalization were less impacted. The reason is that highly digitalized
companies, through DevOps practices, optimize process-driven and data-driven procedures to
enhance new technological infrastructure capabilities via value delivery. At the same time, they
facilitate application modernization practices, improving efficiency and multi-cloud portability
via modern infrastructure, thereby achieving compatibility between modern applications and
existing applications.
The essence of application modernization is to amend the traditional programming methods
of business applications, making them more closely aligned with the needs of business agility.
During the process of an application’s transition to modernization, the existing information
architecture, operation, and maintenance models, application development and testing processes,
business data management models, and security requirements all face significant challenges.
It’s like changing engines and motors during flight: enterprises must both ensure continuity
of business growth amidst current competition and guarantee the potential for revolutionary
business changes in the future.
Shift-left practices and application modernization help DevOps improve delivery before software
reaches production. However, DevOps must also support what happens after delivery: how
systems are monitored, how feedback is collected, how data is used, and how IT services continue
to support business outcomes. This is where the digital operations capability of DevOps becomes
important.
Strengthening digital operations with DevOps
In traditional concepts, DevOps technical operations mainly focus on scenarios for application
domain assurance and user experience, especially in areas such as user data feedback and
intelligent monitoring, establishing end-to-end data link channels between IT and business sides.
In the context of digital transformation, DevOps technical operations in the IT domain need to
extend and restructure data scenarios to realize the digital reconstruction of business applications.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 174
DevOps technical operations need to consume existing data, collect and inventory the entire data
system, establish and improve a data-driven system, and, while improving efficiency and quality,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 173
chunks.content:
extend the ability to deliver data output to the entire IT process by taking a digital operations-
oriented approach. This helps enhance IT service capability, allowing IT organizations to provide
more effective services to customers in advance through a “data role.”
There are two approaches to DevOps technical operations within the IT domain: one is to achieve
business-defined technical operations, and the other is to achieve user-defined technical
operations.
Achieving business-defined technical operations
In the process of digital transformation, IT organizations need the capability to identify business
use cases, especially in the digital technology domain, and should keep up with trends in business
applications. For C-end business scenarios, more attention should be paid to the impact of digital
factors of “people” and “technology” on customer behavior in order to define business scenarios.
Therefore, DevOps capabilities should center around the definition of business scenarios, adapting
IT organizations and IT culture to achieve better, faster, and more effective business support. At
the same time, in the DevOps value delivery pipeline, IT organizational capabilities should focus
on business scenarios, using requirement shift-left and testing shift-left practices to analyze
the value and impact of the delivery process on business use cases and promptly optimize the
supporting capabilities of the IT organization.
Business-defined technical operations represent the top-level design for technological digital
transformation within IT organizations under DevOps, used to realize the rapid launch of
enterprise-strategic products.
Implementing user-defined technology operations
User definition requires focusing more on user scenarios, aligning value output with the IT
organizational architecture in terms of user experience, especially in customer-facing TOC (To
Customer) scenarios. User-defined technology operations empower infrastructure and application
architecture through DevOps, adapting to more flexible user interaction modes, enhancing user
stickiness, obtaining the fastest feedback from the user side, and achieving lifecycle management
of user behavior through user data analysis. This continuously optimizes the IT system’s service
capabilities, as shown in Figure 6.4.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 175
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 175
Figure 6.4: DevOps empowerment methods
In terms of infrastructure, represented by DevOps integrated cloud management platforms, user
scenarios and resource output are formed into a closed loop, supporting the overall business
operation from a technical perspective. This ensures that business development and infrastructure
remain aligned, and IT costs can be allocated to business operations, thus reducing costs from
a business perspective.
In terms of application architecture, represented by DevOps integrated microservices architectures,
the service-oriented business model integration architecture is transformed into a unified agile
architecture. By means of microservices, user-defined scenarios are broken down into smaller
unit services. Through flexible inter-service interaction and collaboration, business changes can
be rapidly supported, enhancing the product’s ability to respond to high-frequency changes in
user interaction.
These business-defined and user-defined operations capabilities depend on more than data and
technical platforms. They also require teams to collaborate flexibly across departments, processes,
and tools as business needs change. This collaborative flexibility is another important DevOps
capability.
Enabling elastic collaboration through DevOps
DevOps’ elastic collaboration model is based on DevOps culture, breaking down communication
and collaboration barriers horizontally across departments and integrating people, processes, and
technology vertically, ultimately achieving continuous organizational improvement.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 176
DevOps introduces the cultural thinking of “value delivery” and “digital operations.” On the IT
side, digital value is extended, forming a closed loop in responding to market changes and feedback
through product delivery. This ultimately drives enterprises to reduce costs and increase efficiency
across a series of business stages, including market demand, product demand, product marketing,
and market feedback, achieving the desired goals. Under this collaboration model, the scope of
elasticity is related to how business changes occur. As the best accelerator for modern business
transformation, DevOps makes it easier for enterprises to adopt and rapidly realize business
ideas during digital transformation.
At the same time, in terms of personnel, process, and technology, DevOps continually and rapidly
delivers new value to customers through a more scientific collaboration approach, making
products better adapt to the ever-changing market and conveying the organization’s digital
profile to customers. When people, processes, and technology are aligned with the same business
goals, the digital transformation process becomes orderly and stable. Additionally, DevOps, via

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 175
chunks.content:
data-driven methods, carries out IT-side technical operations surrounding “people, finance, and
material” to achieve end-to-end delivery of resources, products, and value. This enables unified
resource planning and cost review, providing flexible collaboration for IT organizations regarding
task prioritization and resource scheduling.
DevOps’ role in digital transformation helps IT organizations improve efficiency, enhance
competitive posture, and increase participation in production activities, aiding the shift from
traditional hierarchical, command-and-control enterprises to digital organizations.
Business going online
A Business going online is a key milestone in software delivery. The type of enterprise, digital
scenarios, and transformation goals are always anchored to business value and company
operations, ultimately culminating in a business going online. On the IT side, this is usually
measured by “business continuity” indicators. For enterprises, the transition from offline to
online and the availability assurance of core systems are essential. For IT organizations, faster
and better product delivery, as well as more stable and higher-quality product maintenance, all
fall within the realm of business online.
Data-driven
The transformation of internal and external management and operation models in enterprises
through data-driven approaches usually involves two methods: First, evolving from process-
driven to data-driven, ensuring process compliance while improving the scientific nature of
execution and decision-making through data feedback; second, using data collaboration to mine
better business logic and organizational management models.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 177
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 177
This is particularly evident in digital marketing and digital office fields, where shifts in user
relationships can be detected sensitively, and more scientific, compliant, and agile workflows
and standards can be built using labeling methods.
While data-driven collaboration improves visibility and decision-making, it also exposes new
risks. If delivery, testing, security, and user-experience data are incomplete or delayed, DevOps
teams may make decisions without enough evidence. For this reason, digital risk management
becomes an important part of mature DevOps practice.
Digital risk capabilities in DevOps
By analyzing best practice cases in DevOps, the author believes that digital risk is not limited only
to the measurement and feedback phase. The lack of advanced scenario-based testing data, end-to-
end security data, and the universality of user experience prediction are all manifestations of digital
risk. Common digital risk scenarios mainly include effectiveness evaluation of IT organizations,
post-evaluation and cost review of IT projects, and feedback and assurance in product operations.
Due to the characteristics of the DevOps culture, the collaborative environment and shared
responsibility model among IT members transmit product issues, which are ultimately reflected
in business scenarios through product operations. This is both an advantage of DevOps and a
potential risk factor in practice.
Lack of advanced scenario-based testing data
Testing is a critical link in the DevOps capability subdomain, responsible for the acceptance of
“product-level” deliverables—especially in the shift-left testing phase, where quality extends
to business requirements. Therefore, testing is essential for verifying whether applications or
services behave as expected and whether products can be delivered safely.
A lack of advanced scenario-based testing data often results in issues with stability and accuracy
in testing outcomes during value delivery, thus impacting product quality and safety. For digital-
assisted decision-making, complete testing data can simulate data changes and user conversion
journeys in business operations in advance. These advanced scenarios are oriented toward business
and requirements organizations while providing predictive positive feedback to digital users.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 178
End-to-end security data
By embedding security data into the DevOps “value delivery” chain through risk mitigation, risks
in the product delivery process can be effectively avoided, thereby amplifying the advantages of
DevOps. End-to-end security data allows for continuous monitoring of data performance during
software delivery and product operation. Through comprehensive visibility into service delivery
infrastructure, applications, their interdependencies, and intelligent business data analytics,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 177
chunks.content:
it is possible to address potential threats before they impact business operations. At the same
time, the end-to-end security data covers all nodes in the product operation process, delivering
intelligence, and public opinion feedback in business language from the business perspective,
promoting digital visibility, and secure telemetry in digital operations.
Universality prediction of user experience
Traditional DevOps practices tend to focus more on requirements fulfillment and delivery cycles.
With the continuous evolution of user habits, the aggregation effect between DevOps and business
organizations is increasingly prominent, particularly in terms of the universality prediction of
user experience. According to authoritative statistics, user experience mainly centers on high
expectations of functionality and low tolerance for issues. Therefore, DevOps requires preemptive
digital feedback, covering user experience scenarios. From the user’s perspective, digital scenarios
should be extended to business planning, product requirements, testing data, release strategies,
and final business monitoring, enabling a comprehensive understanding of the business and
focusing on user experience, bringing in, and managing the visibility of the user experience
through digital visualization.
As DevOps practices mature, the same principles of automation, monitoring, feedback, and
lifecycle management are being extended to AI systems. This shift has led to related practices
such as MLOps and LLMOps, which adapt DevOps thinking to the development, deployment,
monitoring, and governance of machine learning and LLM applications.
DevOps in the era of LLMs
With the development of artificial intelligence technologies, more innovative technologies have
been introduced into the Ops field. Currently, there are two main directions: machine learning
and LLMs, which have ultimately led to MLOps (Machine Learning Operations) and LLMOps.
This chapter focuses on MLOps as a discipline — how the model-development work -
flow integrates with DevOps practice. The model-training techniques themselves
were covered in Chapter 4 (fine-tuning) and Chapter 5 (RAG and multi-agent systems).

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 179
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 179
The origin of MLOps
MLOps is a concept evolved from DevOps, referring to the application of DevOps ideas and
methods to the development, deployment, and operation and maintenance of machine learning,
aiming to improve the productivity and quality of machine learning models.
The concept of MLOps originated from the challenges enterprises faced when applying machine
learning in practice, mainly involving issues such as model deployment, operation and maintenance,
and monitoring. In traditional software development, a mature DevOps process has already been
established, and MLOps borrows from DevOps experience and thinking within the field of machine
learning to provide systematic and standardized solutions for machine learning development.
The MLOps process includes multiple stages such as data preparation, model selection, model
training, model deployment, model validation, and model updating, as shown in Figure 6.5.
Figure 6.5: Sequence of MLOps processes
Once the origin of MLOps is clear, the next question is how it changes the responsibilities of
DevOps teams in practice. MLOps keeps the core DevOps focus on automation, monitoring, and
continuous improvement, but extends it to the additional lifecycle needs of machine learning
systems.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 180
The role of MLOps
In practical application, based on the characteristics of machine learning, the role of MLOps—
beyond the traditional capabilities of DevOps—has added some specific scenarios, such as
redefining scenarios via model application, data collection, and organization, model training
and deployment, as well as continuous monitoring and updating. Nevertheless, the iteration, and
updating of technology are all aimed at improving the efficiency of software delivery.
Since MLOps originates from DevOps, the core philosophies of both are the same, covering
the initial tool-oriented and automated stages of construction, and sharing common paths for
optimization and feedback during adoption. However, there are also some differences: due to
differences in tech stacks, the trigger targets and methods differ. The trigger method for DevOps is
mainly code modification, while MLOps triggers are not limited to code changes—changes in data
or a decline in model performance (model degradation) can also trigger the pipeline. In addition,
MLOps includes additional steps necessary for building and training machine learning models,
such as data- and model-specific procedures, which means that there are subtle differences in
each component of the MLOps workflow.
In addition, in terms of workflow management, DevOps focuses on pipeline construction, while
MLOps emphasizes more on the management and automation of machine learning workflows,
as well as model deployment and monitoring.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 179
chunks.content:
MLOps workflow based on DevOps
As shown in Figure 6.6, a standard MLOps workflow involves three roles: data engineer, model
engineer, and DevOps engineer.
Figure 6.6: Standard MLOps workflow

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 181
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 181
Data engineers are responsible for data annotation and ensuring data reliability and traceability;
model engineers are responsible for model management and ensuring model reproducibility
and iterability; DevOps engineers are responsible for application deployment and monitoring.
1. The main work in the data stage includes data collection, preprocessing, and feature
engineering:
• Data collection and preprocessing: This component is responsible for collecting
data from various sources (such as databases, file systems, APIs, etc.) and
performing preprocessing and cleaning, making the data suitable for training
and inference with machine learning models.
• Feature engineering: This component is responsible for transforming raw data
into features usable by machine learning models, including steps such as feature
selection, feature transformation, and feature construction.
2. The main tasks in the model stage include model training, model deployment, and model
monitoring and management:
• Model training: This component is responsible for training models using the
training data, including algorithm selection, model parameter tuning, and model
performance evaluation.
• Model deployment: This component is responsible for deploying trained models
to the production environment for real-time inference and prediction. It may
include steps such as packaging the model as an executable file, configuring the
model server, and monitoring model performance.
• Model monitoring and management: This component is responsible for
monitoring the performance and operating status of deployed models and making
adjustments and updates as needed. It may include monitoring metrics such as
model prediction accuracy, processing time, and resource usage.
3. The main work in the deployment stage is software release:
Although model output is uncertain and difficult to reproduce, the process of deploying
machine learning software to the production environment is reliable and repeatable and
aims to be as automated as possible.
MLOps provides a useful foundation for managing machine learning systems, but LLM-powered
applications introduce additional challenges, including prompt management, retrieval pipelines,
evaluation, model behavior monitoring, cost control, and governance. These differences have led
to the emergence of LLMOps.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 182
The origin of LLMOps
LLMOps is a set of tools and best practices for managing the lifecycle of LLM-powered applications.
It can be seen as a subcategory of MLOps, but there are certain differences between the two. These
differences stem from the different ways of building AI products with classic ML models versus
LLMs, primarily impacting data management, experimentation, evaluation, and cost.
DevOps improves software delivery by strengthening collaboration, automation, visibility,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 181
chunks.content:
feedback, and lifecycle management. However, as organizations scale, teams often need a
more structured way to access the tools, environments, workflows, and infrastructure required
for delivery. This is where platform engineering becomes important: it turns shared delivery
capabilities into reusable internal platforms that reduce cognitive load and help teams deliver
software more consistently.
Building internal platforms for software delivery
Platform engineering extends DevOps practices by turning shared tools, infrastructure, workflows,
and knowledge into reusable internal platforms. Its goal is to reduce cognitive load for delivery
teams, improve developer experience, and make software delivery more consistent, secure, and
scalable.
The concept of platform engineering
Gartner describes platform engineering as gathering tools, capabilities, and processes—all
meticulously selected and packaged by domain experts—into a platform for end users. The
ultimate goal is to create a frictionless self-service experience, providing users with adequate
capabilities to complete critical tasks at minimal cost, thus increasing end-user productivity and
reducing cognitive load. The platform should meet all the needs of user teams and seamlessly fit
their preferred workflows in any possible form.
In the software delivery process, platform engineering aims to improve the efficiency and
effectiveness of software delivery teams, enabling enterprises to gain greater competitive
advantages in the market. By building a suite of tool platforms, software delivery teams can
deliver software application systems more efficiently and continuously, while ensuring their stable
operation. The core goal of platform engineering is to help software delivery teams enhance the
business value of the software they deliver.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 183
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 183
Within the software delivery system, platform engineering addresses how technical teams can
meet business needs at lower cost and with higher efficiency, while also solving various issues
in efficient business operations and enterprise digital transformation. Therefore, the value of
platform engineering lies in the infrastructure capabilities it provides, as well as the technical
services of the corresponding tool clusters. By using tool platforms to consolidate knowledge,
software delivery teams can improve overall efficiency and innovation.
The value of platform engineering in the software delivery process is reflected in the following
aspects:
• Reusability: Platform engineering has the capability for modular assembly. The technical
components and services provided by platform engineering can be shared and reused
across multiple applications, thus avoiding repetitive development and maintenance of
similar functions.
• Centralized Capability: Platform engineering possesses the ability to centrally manage
and monitor tools across domains. Users can more easily manage software applications
and the delivery process through tools, and use tools to maintain the entire application
lifecycle, thereby increasing the efficiency of software delivery and ensuring its stability.
• Scalability: Platform engineering integrates cloud-native capabilities, allowing the
elastically scalable cloud-native infrastructure to expand and upgrade smoothly and
quickly according to customer needs, in order to meet constantly changing business
requirements.
• Security: Platform engineering possesses security features, allowing software delivery
personnel to protect the security of applications and customer data through authentication,
authorization, and security services provided by platform engineering, thereby reducing
security risks.
After defining platform engineering and explaining its value in software delivery, the next step is
to identify the qualities that make an internal platform effective. A useful platform is not simply
a collection of tools; it must be designed as a product that supports user needs, reduces friction,
enables self-service, and helps teams share knowledge across the delivery lifecycle.
Key attributes of platform engineering
Generally, software delivery teams can provide a better user experience by combining one or more
capabilities through a mature, available, and promotable platform. Such platforms enable their
users to deliver valuable products more easily and efficiently.
Building a Modern Software Delivery Foundation 184
An excellent platform typically has the key attributes discussed as follows:
Platform as a product
In the field of software delivery, the platform needs to meet the needs of all users as much as
possible. These needs must cover all functional organizations in the delivery pipeline, and each

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 183
chunks.content:
functional organization should have corresponding requirements based on its own responsibilities.
The platform should be designed according to these requirements, and scalability considerations
should be included in the design.
Similar to other software products, the platform must provide the necessary functions for each
functional organization to support common use cases for cross-functional teams, and these use
cases should be prioritized to ensure continuity of functionality when single or multiple teams
collaborate, guaranteeing the ultimate value of software delivery. In practical application, the
author prefers the collaborative state shown in Figure 6.7.
Figure 6.7: Positive feedback loop of Platform Engineering
Team structure and working models should rely on the platform to implement agile software
delivery. Platform architects should possess full life cycle thinking, ensuring the platform has
self-service capabilities, covering R&D delivery processes and business assurance processes.
Product managers should rely on the platform to shift their focus from “system processes” to
“business experience” to better connect product requirements with the process of launching
applications. Others should provide feedback on issues and pain points encountered during
platform usage to the platform architect, ultimately forming a positive feedback loop through
optimization.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 6 185
chunks.content:
Chapter 6 185
User experience
The platform should improve user experience through a unified interface and continually focus on
user experience during platform design, which is crucial for promoting the platform. The platform
should strive to meet the needs of all users. The author explains with examples using common
tools: During the tool integration stage, platform architects need to consider combinations of
commonly used GUIs, APIs, and command line tools, and think about the presentation forms of
IDEs and portals. Typically, the platform provides deployment capabilities to enable application
deployment during development. In many enterprises, developers often use IDEs, testers may
use command line tools, while product personnel may use GUI-based web portals. The above
approaches may lead to user experience issues, so it is particularly important to build a developer
platform with a product mindset.
In some enterprises that have not yet implemented platform engineering, during the delivery
process of a certain project, when developers submit service requests to the platform architect
to improve certain slow and inflexible service flows, the platform architect usually coordinates
